vignette: Kofi's eyes would glaze over whenever his partner, Ama, asked about his childhood. He had grown accustomed to avoiding conversations that might lead him down a path of memories he'd rather not confront. But on days when the school was particularly chaotic, and he found himself struggling to maintain order among the students, old photos would resurface in his mind - images of him as a young boy, cowering in fear as his caregiver's rage escalated. It wasn't just the memories themselves that were unsettling; it was the way they seemed to seep into his present. Waking up from a nightmare, Kofi would be convinced that he could still feel the weight of his caregiver's hand on his skin, and for a moment, the line between past and present would blur. He'd try to shake off the feeling, telling himself it was just a dream, but as he went about his day, fragments of memories would resurface - disconnected pieces that refused to fit together into a coherent narrative. Kofi had come to believe that these fragmented memories were a sign of permanent damage, evidence that he'd been irreparably changed by the abuse. He felt helpless against the resurgence of these memories, unable to stop them from flooding his mind and threatening to derail his carefully constructed sense of self-control. As the principal of a school, Kofi prided himself on being able to manage even the most unruly of students, but when faced with unpredictable situations - a sudden outburst in the classroom or an unexpected confrontation with a parent - he'd feel a familiar surge of anxiety. The more these memories recurred, the more real they seemed. They felt more vivid than his memories of ordinary things, like the way Ama smiled on their first date or the sound of the ocean during their summer vacation. And with each recurrence, Kofi became increasingly convinced that he was capable of unleashing a similar brand of rage upon those around him - that he was just one misstep away from losing control entirely. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Kofi began to notice a change in his behavior. He found himself growing more withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings and opting instead for solitary evenings spent scrolling through old photos on his phone. It was as if he'd become trapped in a cycle of avoidance, constantly trying to outrun the memories that haunted him. One evening, as Ama confronted Kofi about his increasingly distant behavior, he realized that something had to change. He couldn't continue living in fear of his own memories, nor could he keep pushing away those who cared for him most. With a sense of trepidation, Kofi finally made the decision to seek help - not just for himself, but for those around him whom he feared might one day bear the brunt of his unbridled rage. For now, though, as he sat in his office, staring blankly at the old photos on his phone, Kofi couldn't shake the feeling that he was trapped in a never-ending cycle - one from which he wasn't sure he'd ever be able to escape.
